doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: His own records and career today
title: Rural Still Life quartet album and the Spahn Ranch cover
summary: His second Impulse album was a jazz quartet record; the cover cabin became the Manson family home.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well there was a time, especially in the 50s and 60s where you could have an instrumental hit, you know “Cast Your Fate to the Wind” and “Stranger on the Shore.”
Vince Guaraldi. I remember them all well.

But when you got to the point where you had a reputation and you were doing solo recordings, I’m wondering how much thought did you give to fitting into what niche? Was it going to be jazz-rock, was it — or maybe this didn’t even occur to you. Maybe you were just composing music and looking for tunes that you liked?

Pretty much the latter. I was in New York, I can’t remember why, but I got to see Bob Thiele in his office at Impulse Records at the time, and it was time to do another, a second album. And he said, “Tom what do you want to do?” And I said, “I want to do a jazz album with my quartet” which at the time was Mike Lang on piano, Chuck Domanico on bass and John Guerin on drums. And so he said, “Cool.” So back in Los Angeles I walked into United Recording Studio. Bob was in the booth and his engineer, a guy named Eddie Bracken, I’ll never forget him ‘cause boy I don’t know whether he was on stimulants or what he was doing but he was like at that board and he — and in those days it was like rotary pots, it went like this — round knobs that you turned for volume up and down. And he’d sit there at that board and he’d — oh man, the guy’s going to have a heart attack. I think eventually he did. But anyway so I went in there with my quartet and made what I considered to be a jazz album. I mean it was a jazz album. And there’s a funny story connected with that actually which involves the shooting of the cover. The cover was determined by Bob — well the title of the album was determined to be Rural Still Life which was the opening track of the album, a tune that Mike Lang had written. So I got a call from the photographer one day, he says, “Listen, Bob Thiele has asked me to shoot your cover and he told me it’s ‘Rural Still Life’” so he says, “I know this place out in the north San Fernando Valley where they have horses and cabins and sort of a western little community.” So he said, “Let’s go out there, bring your band and we’ll find a place to shoot the cover with the band.” I said, “Great.” So we found this cabin, this unoccupied cabin, and we posed in front of it and took the picture which became the cover of the record “Rural Still Life.” About six months later that cabin and that surrounding area became the home of the Charles Manson family. It was the Spahn Movie Ranch.
And we got out of there just in time I always like to say.
So that probably increases the value of that LP if you can find it.
Well you know very few people know about that story except the ones I have told.
